Lessons.Title: Name the Parts
ExplanationParagraphs: Fractions represent equal-size (equal-AREA) parts of one whole. Merely having two pieces is NOT sufficient to call them halves; the parts must be equal in area. Shapes can be partitioned in many ways.

Original warm-up 2021 Which One Doesn't Belong: A rectangle diagonally split into two equal triangles; B rectangle split into two equal vertical parts with one shaded; C circle divided by a diameter into equal semicircles; D rectangle with off-center cut into two UNEQUAL parts. Pupils may justify any distinguishing trait; important original insight is D's pieces are not halves.

Activity1 original Card Sort: Partitions features twelve SOURCE-labelled figures mapped by reading actual original HTML figure-label/image pairs. A circle2 equal; B square4 equal; C rectangle2 unequal; D circle4 equal; E square2 equal (horizontal); F rectangle2 equal (vertical); G rectangle3 equal (horizontal strips); H circle3 unequal; I square2 unequal (off-corner diagonal); J circle3 equal (sectors); K rectangle3 equal (vertical strips); L rectangle4 equal (vertical strips).

Original student instructions say sort A–L into ANY TWO teacher-defended categories of your choosing, not necessarily equal/unequal. An appropriate specific distinction to elicit is equal A,B,D,E,F,G,J,K,L, versus unequal C,H,I. Category membership is not a unique graded scalar; teacher examines explanation, shape and equal AREA.

Activity2 original Fold and Name: each student folds four copied paper rectangles into3,6,4,8 equal parts, draws fold lines, talks with partner and names thirds1/3, sixths1/6, fourths1/4, eighths1/8. Folding into thirds then halves gives sixths; folding into fourths then halves gives eighths.

Synthesis also reviews halves1/2 and labels each equal-area piece of a whole. Fractions consist of a numerator1 (one part selected) and denominator n (whole split into n equal parts), for n2,3,4,6,8. Original source single fraction-strip example showed two equal halves.

Original 17 unique figure assets inspected visually on owner device; Edulytics diagrams are newly generated educational equivalents, never publisher SVG source paths. Original blackline paper sheet and publisher-gated Partition a Rectangle Cool-down not certified; Stage D and runtime tests unrun.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole and parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: One shape or region is the whole; dividing it creates parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Only equal-area parts are named unit fractions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Bottom fraction number tells number of equal parts in the whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 1/n for one of n equal parts

KeyConcepts.Title: Numerator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Top fraction number describes how many equal parts are selected.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One selected equal part has numerator1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal area, any arrangement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Regions need not have the same outline orientation; their areas must be equal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Different shapes/partitions can represent the same unit fraction.
KeyConcepts.Example: A diagonal rectangle can have two equal-area halves.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up off-center
WorkedExamples.Question: Can two UNEQUAL pieces of one rectangle both be called halves?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal-area regions and represent one part as a unit fraction.
Steps: Two pieces are visible but not same area.
Halves must be two equal-area parts.
Compare each region's area, not simply the number of pieces: unequal regions cannot both be halves.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Card B
WorkedExamples.Question: Square quartered by centered horizontal and vertical segments.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal-area regions and represent one part as a unit fraction.
Steps: Each piece is one of four equal-area regions, and four quarters reconstruct the whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Card J
WorkedExamples.Question: Circle into three equal sectors.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal-area regions and represent one part as a unit fraction.
Steps: Three equal one-third sectors reconstruct the whole: 3 × (1/3) = 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fold sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Make six equal areas in a rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal-area regions and represent one part as a unit fraction.
Steps: Halve each equal third to produce six equal areas.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fold eighths
WorkedExamples.Question: Make eight equal areas in a rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal-area regions and represent one part as a unit fraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Label unequal pieces 1/2 because there are two.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal AREA, not number only, is necessary for halves.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Cards C and I, and warm-up D, demonstrate off-center cuts.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Force every card sort into a unique official two-category answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original student task allows any justified pair of sorting criteria.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Grade rationale and ensure one teacher activity highlights equal vs unequal.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confuse 1/6 denominator with six selected parts.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Six names equal parts in the whole; one is selected.

SummaryPoints: Original warm-up D unequal; A/B/C equal halves.
